name: Bunaq
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Schapper, Antoinette. 2009 [Glottolog dates it 2010]. Bunaq: a Papuan language of central Timor. PhD thesis, Australian National University, Canberra. xxxviii+549 pp. hdl:1885/150147 (open ANU repository scan with). Chapter 2 'Phonology and morphophonology' is explicitly 'a preliminary account of the phonology of the Lamaknen dialect of Bunaq'.
catalog_locator: §2.4 Stress, thesis pp. 62-64; 'Stress is not phonemic' in the Abstract and §1.9.1 (typological overview; ch. 1 typology table row '7 Stress: penultimate stress'); reduplication §2.5.5 p. 68 (ex. 58); compounds ['meaq 'gol] and fused dikotel in the compounding section; /erenoq/ stress shift §2.3; Tetun loans hatama, ['hatun].
catalog_quote: [p. 62] 2.4 Stress. In my preliminary analysis of Bunaq stress, stress appears to fall regularly on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word, as in the following disyllabic (46) and trisyllabic words (47). 46. ˈtekeʔ 'look at' ˈpana 'woman' ˈbini 'steal' [p. 63] 47. buˈleʔen ... hoˈnogo 'be separate' koˈroroʔ 'cheer'. In words of four syllables primary stress still falls on the penultimate syllable. There also appears to be a secondary stress that falls on the initial syllable (48). ... 48. ˌsiruˈbisu 'work' ˌbereˈlikuʔ 'k.o. bird' ˌhileˈrenoʔ 'k.o. bird'. In Bunaq stress is assigned before the application of any morphophonological processes to a lexical item. That is, prefixes are extrametrical and are not counted in stress assignment rules. ... 49. gV- + ˈul 'extract' = gˈul ... gV- + ˈbul 'base' = guˈbul ... The penultimate stress analysis is based upon elicitation of words in isolation. In discourse, however, it is apparent that the place of a word in an intonation unit can [p. 64] effect its realisation. In particular, for many items it is possible to reduce or entirely omit the apparently lexically accented syllable in particular phrasal positions. ... The prevalence of such behaviour could mean that lexical accents are 'ignored' for the purposes of intonation in Bunaq. Alternatively, Bunaq may lack lexical accent altogether. The nature of stress in Bunaq and its relationship to intonation remains to be investigated.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word (root), counted before prefixation; prefixes are extrametrical so a prefixed monosyllabic root keeps stress on the root. Non-phonemic. Described as preliminary, from words in isolation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Apparent secondary stress on the initial syllable of four-syllable words (e.g.,iru'bisu 'work'); perceptually louder than unstressed syllables, but phonetic correlates not established because four-syllable items are very few (p. 63).
new_statements.exceptions: Prefixes (e.g. 3an gV-) are extrametrical: g-'ul, gu-'bul, ge-'teke? keep root stress (p. 63). Reduplication: 'Each reduplicant attracts primary stress' (§2.5). Compounds like meaq gol are two phonological words each with primary stress ['meaq 'gol]; fused compounds (dikotel 'cassava') take a single penultimate stress. /ereno?/ 'day before' may delete its stressed /e/, shifting stress to the new penult (p. 61). Tetun loans (hatama, ['hatun]) are re-stressed on the penult. Determiners/specifiers and halaqi =i are often unstressed in rapid speech.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word; analysis explicitly based on elicitation of words in isolation (p. 63). In discourse the stressed syllable of some words can be reduced or omitted at the end of a 'continuing' intonation unit with a high final tonal target, so the author allows that 'lexical accents are ignored for the purposes of intonation' or that 'Bunaq may lack lexical accent altogether' (p. 64, fn. 6 citing Himmelmann on Waima'a). Abstract and ch. 1 state 'Stress is not phonemic.'
new_statements.identity_note: Schapper 2009 §2.4 describes the Lamaknen dialect of Bunaq (Belu regency, Indonesian side; ch. 2 is explicitly 'a preliminary account of the phonology of the Lamaknen dialect'); the thesis notes consonant inventories differ by dialect (Lamaknen vs Lolotoen). Glottolog buna1278 has no dialect-level codes. Berthe 1963 calls the language Buna' (Timor central); the variety is not specified on the page opened.

new_statements.quote: Enfin, notons que la langue ne connaît pas, à la différence du Tétun voisin par exemple, d'accent à valeur phonologique; elle ignore de même l'accent tonique à valeur prosodique.
new_statements.translation: Finally, let us note that the language does not have, unlike neighbouring Tetun for example, an accent with phonological value; it likewise lacks a tonic (stress) accent with prosodic value.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (Schapper 2009 PhD §2.4, pp. 62-64, verified in the text we hold: 'stress appears to fall regularly on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word.. secondary stress.. on the initial syllable'; abstract: 'Stress is not phonemic') gives fixed penultimate stress. Berthe 1959 agrees on the one point that accent is not phonemic/distinctive in Bunaq, but goes further and denies any tonic accent 'à valeur prosodique', i.e. a no-word-stress claim, which differs in TYPE from a regular penultimate stress. new_statements.rule_in_words: Berthe states in one sentence that Bunaq (Lamaknen) has no accent with phonological (distinctive) value, unlike neighbouring Tetun, and moreover no 'accent tonique' with prosodic value at all, i.e. he reports no word stress. No placement rule, no examples with stress marks, no further discussion; the phonology section is one page (consonant and vowel inventories, word shape of one to two syllables, rarely three, no consonant clusters, diphthongs).
new_statements.exceptions: none; the only qualification is dialectal (fn. 5: Mau-Gatal on the Portuguese side differs in the realisation of d), which concerns segments, not accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Berthe 1959 describes the Buna' of Lamaknen, Indonesian (western) central Timor (fn. 5 p. 349 and p. 350: phonological notation reflects Lamaknen pronunciation only; Mau-Gatal on the Portuguese side differs in the realisation of d). Schapper 2009's phonology chapter is likewise a preliminary account of the Lamaknen dialect. Same language as Glottolog buna1278 / ISO bfn (Bunaq, Bunak, Buna', Marae).

readall_conflicts: Berthe 1959 (p. 349) says Bunaq has no accent with phonological value and 'ignore de même l'accent tonique à valeur prosodique', a no-word-stress claim; the catalog record and the verified statement held by the project (Schapper 2009 PhD §2.4, pp. 62-64) give regular penultimate primary stress with initial secondary stress in four-syllable words, stress not phonemic. The two agree that stress/accent is not distinctive; they disagree on whether there is a (predictable) word accent at all. Berthe's remark is a single sentence without data in a 1959 article on sung distichs; Schapper's is a dedicated, exemplified (preliminary) analysis of the same Lamaknen variety fifty years later, so the fixed-penultimate reading stays best supported and Berthe 1959 is an early dissenting note to record, not a replacement. Schapper 2022 (A grammar of Bunaq, De Gruyter, ch. 2) remains unread and paywalled and would settle the current description.
